briefs.headline: Women's Hockey World Cup: India look to sign off with Germany test
briefs.deck: Having played five matches so far, India have won one, drawn three and lost only once — against hosts Netherlands.
briefs.bodyText:
The Indian women’s hockey team will look to end their World Cup campaign on a high when they face Germany in the fifth-sixth place classification match at Wagener Hockey Stadium in Amstelveen on Thursday.
Having played five matches so far, India have won one, drawn three and lost only once — against hosts Netherlands. It has been an impressive campaign for a team that looked out of sorts last year, and coach Sjoerd Marijne has been more than pleased with the progress his wards have made.
“I told the girls, ‘If I had told you six months ago that we would play a quarterfinal against Australia at the World Cup and draw 0-0, would you have believed it?’ I don’t think, considering the position they were in six months ago, they would have believed it,” said Marijne in a video released by Hockey India.
Indeed, India have produced a fascinating campaign, with almost everyone contributing at different stages. The only glaring gap has been their inability to convert chances into goals consistently — something that eventually ended their hopes of reaching the semifinals.
“We have really made good progress, and it’s not easy to score goals against these teams. The basis of our game is our defence, and we do that really well,” Marijne said.
Apart from their games against China and South Africa, India failed to score against England, Netherlands and Australia. It was not for a lack of opportunities, but rather their inability to make those chances count when it mattered most.
That will once again be put to the test against Germany, coached by a familiar face in former India head coach Janneke Schopman.
Germany, too, have been through a transition since the Paris Olympics and could not make the semifinals after losing their two crucial matches against Argentina and Belgium. They did, however, win three matches across the two rounds, while scoring 13 goals in the process.
Their ability to find the net has been one of their biggest positives, but breaking down India’s defence could prove a different challenge.
Schopman knows this Indian team well from her time as their head coach and is likely to have plenty of insight into how to exploit their weaknesses. However, India have shown they can be extremely difficult to break down when they get their defensive structure right.
England had 20 shots on goal and 12 penalty corners in their 0-0 draw with India, while Australia managed 13 shots and five penalty corners in India's last game. Neither could find a way past the Indian defence.
Speaking about the Australia match, Marijne said, “We evaluated the game with the team, and sometimes these things happen in a process. Sometimes you take a step back to make two steps forward. But again, we didn’t lose; we just didn’t win.”
India may not be playing for a medal, but Thursday’s game offers them one final opportunity to underline the progress they have made at the World Cup.
A strong finish against Germany would also give the team valuable confidence heading into the Asian Games, where a gold medal would bring with it a direct qualification spot for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

briefs.headline: Northeast's first GM, 17-yo Mayank and pupil Pratitee become Asia's chess champions
briefs.deck: A remarkable teacher-student story from the Asian Junior Chess Championships, where India’s 94th GM and Northeast’s first GM, 17-year-old Mayank Chakraborty, and his 13-year-old pupil Pratitee Bordoloi won the classical titles in Mumbai. The story explores their three-month mentoring journey, the pressure of being top seeds, Pratitee’s WGM norm, and Mayank’s rise while balancing his own career…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Mayank Chakraborty became India's 94th Grandmaster and the first from the Northeast region last March. He is still 17, but talking to him, however, gives away very little about his age; he sounds more like a man with years of experience on his shoulders.
On Tuesday, he added another feather to his cap, lifting the coveted classical title at the Asian Junior Chess Championships in Mumbai. In the girls' category, 13-year-old Pratitee Bordoloi clinched the title on the very same day.
Chakraborty is from Assam. Bordoloi is based out of Bengaluru. However, for the past three-odd months, the distance hasn't mattered much. Chakraborty has been mentoring her, and it found a fairytale moment when both of them walked away champions from the same hall that only hosted Asia's some of the best players under the age of 20.
"Obviously, I became the champion; that's the best thing that happened to me," Chakraborty told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction. "But also one of my students managed to become the champion. It increases my happiness."
Expanding on their preparation together, he added, "I've been mentoring her for almost three to four months now, and I started it all the way in World Youth in Monte Silvano, Italy."
In Italy, Bordoloi clinched silver and became India's only medallist at the 2026 FIDE World Youth Chess Championship. On Tuesday, nevertheless, it was gold, along with a WGM (Women's Grandmaster) norm, which came without much help from her mentor during the tournament.
"During the tournament, it was a bit difficult because he was also playing, but before the tournament he helped me, specifically in preparing openings," an elated Pratitee told this website.
Coming into the tournament as the No. 1 seed, Bordoloi felt the pressure. Her mother, Pranti Dutta Bordoloi, didn't dress it up.
"If I tell you no pressure, I think it will be totally lie," she said. "Whenever you play as the top seed, automatically, whether you want it or not, you will be under pressure. It's like you're giving someone a one-kilo weight on their head and telling them that they have to run now, and they have to come first."
Chakraborty, also the No. 1 seed, had already won the Asian Junior Rapid title once before. But classical, he made clear, is the one that actually counts.
"Since Classical is the actual main form where you become World Champion, it's like I prove my superiority over everyone else," he added.
Further explaining what it means to get his hands on the title, the teenager added, "Rapid Championship ends in one day, and this Classical Championship is a battle for six to seven days. So more hard work, more pressure... Classical chess requires a lot of opening preparation, mental training and all this stuff which Rapid chess doesn't require. Just play. Rapid chess is just about playing."
Struggle is still going on. Same struggle, same life.
Mayank Chakraborty on life since becoming a Grandmaster
Perhaps life has not changed much since becoming a Grandmaster for Mayank, as he muttered, "Struggle is still going on. Same struggle, same life."
However, amid the "struggle", he still finds the room to mentor. How? He said with some palpable confidence, "Honestly, I'm actually very good at multitasking, so I can manage time. I have a timetable, I have a routine, and I follow it very properly. I don't waste time. I don't have any distractions like social media and et cetera. So I can just focus on my work very well."
In the next five days, Chakraborty is scheduled to fly to Turkiye and then Malaysia for chess tournaments abroad. On the other hand, Pratitee and her family are content with the WGM norm and the overall outcome of the Asian Junior C'ships, as her mother concluded, "Honestly speaking, if we do as much as we can in India, it will be very less expensive for us financially," she said. "If we do the same thing outside, it will cost 10 times more money for us."

briefs.headline: Sri Lanka fight after follow-on, but stare at series defeat in Colombo
briefs.deck: After being forced to follow on, Sri Lanka reached 229/6 in their second innings when rain brought an early end to proceedings. With the hosts effectively still 16 runs behind with only four wickets in hand, India require just a final push on the fifth morning to complete victory.
briefs.bodyText:
Sri Lanka’s young guns Pasindu Sooriyabandara and Sonal Dinusha once again emerged as bright spots in an otherwise difficult series, producing gritty knocks to keep the hosts fighting on Day Four of the second Test against India at the Sinhalese Sports Club on Wednesday. Despite their resistance, Sri Lanka remained firmly on the back foot and are staring at a 0-2 series defeat.
After being forced to follow on, Sri Lanka reached 229/6 in their second innings when rain brought an early end to proceedings. With the hosts effectively still 16 runs behind with only four wickets in hand, India require just a final push on the fifth morning to complete victory.
Having already impressed in the first innings with an 80, the 26-year-old Sooriyabandara showcased his growing reputation with a classy 92 off 173 balls, striking 10 fours and a six. He combined with 
Kamindu Mendis
, who made a fighting 55 off 92 deliveries, in a crucial 115-run fourth-wicket partnership that temporarily frustrated the Indian attack and gave Sri Lanka hope of extending the contest.
While India chipped away steadily through the day, Sooriyabandara’s enterprise stood out. Playing only his second Test after making his debut as a concussion substitute in Galle, the right-hander took on India’s most successful bowler of the series, left-arm spinner Manav Suthar, using sweeps, reverse-sweeps and confident footwork to upset the spinner’s rhythm.
His resistance eventually ended on 92 when he charged down the track to Suthar, missed a delivery spinning away outside off stump and was smartly stumped by Rishabh Pant. 
Suthar’s tactical awareness and Pant’s anticipation combined to produce a breakthrough India desperately needed.
Earlier in the day, Sri Lanka resumed their first innings at 265/8, still needing 39 runs to avoid the follow-on. The responsibility once again fell on Dinusha, who continued his remarkable series. Unbeaten overnight on 85, the left-hander completed his second century of the series with a composed 103 off 162 balls, decorated with eight boundaries and three sixes.
Dinusha’s hundred came after scores of 100 and 84 in the opening Test in Galle and underlined his emergence as Sri Lanka’s most dependable batter in the series. A magnificent pull off Prasidh Krishna for four was among the shots of the match as he guided Sri Lanka beyond the follow-on target before the hosts were bowled out for 290 in reply to India’s imposing 503/9 declared.
India’s bowlers, though, ensured the home side never truly seized momentum. Mohammed Siraj struck early in the second innings when opener Lahiru Udara awkwardly fended a bouncer to Saransh Jain at fine leg. Sri Lanka’s opening troubles continued, with their opening partnerships yielding a meagre 46 runs across eight innings in 2026.
Sooriyabandara and Kamil Mishara attempted to counterattack, adding 58 runs in quick time for the second wicket. Mishara looked positive during his 32 from 39 balls before Ravindra Jadeja trapped him leg-before as he missed a sweep.
The standout phase of Sri Lanka’s innings came before lunch, when Sooriyabandara and Kamindu took the score to 162 for two. The pair attacked Suthar aggressively, with Kamindu slog-sweeping and dancing down the track to strike a pair of sixes.
India found inspiration through their captain Shubman Gill. Mendis miscued a pull off Prasidh Krishna and Gill sprinted in from square leg before diving full length to complete a spectacular catch that broke the partnership and swung momentum back India’s way.
Suthar soon struck twice, removing Sooriyabandara and then captain Dhananjaya de Silva for 23. Saransh Jain also played his part, trapping Niroshan Dickwella leg-before as Sri Lanka slipped further.
When rain halted proceedings, Dinusha remained unbeaten on seven alongside Keshav Nuwantha on three. Their task on the final day is daunting, but Sri Lanka will draw encouragement from the performances of Dinusha and Sooriyabandara.

briefs.headline: 88 no-balls! Jadeja’s staggering problem leaves India with a big headache
briefs.deck: Ravindra Jadeja's recurring issue with no-balls has reached alarming levels, tallying 88 infringements since 2021, the most among spinners. This trend intensified following the introduction of television adjudication, during which he was only responsible for 18 no-balls. As the current series unfolds, India's spinners seem to be grappling with discipline and precision, highlighting a need for…
briefs.bodyText:
Ravindra Jadeja
's no-ball problem has become increasingly difficult to ignore, with the India spinner's latest overstepping taking his tally to a staggering 88 in Tests since 2021.
Jadeja bowled three no-balls in the first innings of the ongoing second Test against Sri Lanka and added another in the second innings. His tally during the period is now comfortably the highest among spinners, with Pakistan's Noman Ali a distant second on 40. Lasith Embuldeniya follows with 33, while England's Jack Leach has 19.
Jadeja's issue has become particularly pronounced since television umpires were given the responsibility of calling no-balls during the England-Pakistan Test series in late 2020. Since that change, only Kagiso Rabada, Ben Stokes and 
Jasprit Bumrah
 have bowled more no-balls than Jadeja.
The numbers become even more striking when his career is split into two periods. From his Test debut in 2012 until television adjudication was introduced, Jadeja bowled only 18 no-balls. Since then, he has overstepped 89 times.
The problem has not been restricted to the ongoing Test. In the first Test against Sri Lanka, Jadeja bowled two no-balls in each innings. One proved particularly costly when a delivery that induced Dhananjaya de Silva to edge towards KL Rahul at slip was called a no-ball, giving the Sri Lankan captain a reprieve.
India's spinners have collectively struggled with their discipline in the series. On Day 4 of the Colombo Test, they bowled five no-balls, taking their match tally to 10. While none of those deliveries resulted in a wicket being lost, the frequency has become a concern.

briefs.bodyText:

Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, Angled into the left-hander, on middle. Dinusha pivots on the back foot for the pull but the ball is not all that short. Ekes out an inside edge onto the thigh pad. It drops to the left-hander's right and he is called through for a single.
Saransh Jain to Sonal Dinusha, Hangs it up there, full and on off. Dinusha leans on and drives it to deep cover for one.
Saransh Jain to Sonal Dinusha, At 81.9 kph, full and on off. Dinusha strides forward to defend.
Saransh Jain to Keshara Nuwantha, Slower through the air but the length stays short, on middle. Nuwantha hops back and whips it wide of mid on for a run.
Saransh Jain to Keshara Nuwantha, At 85.4 kph, spinning back in sharply, shorter and on middle. Nuwantha goes deep in the crease and tucks it down in front of short leg.
Saransh Jain to Keshara Nuwantha, Pushed through, full and on off. Nuwantha lunges for the block.
Saransh Jain to Sonal Dinusha, Loopy ball, full and wide on off from around the wicket. Sonal reaches across and drags the sweep to deep square leg for a run.
Prasidh Krishna to Keshara Nuwantha, FOUR! Well played. Prasidh goes searching for the yorker but ends up dishing out a low full toss, on middle. Nuwantha presents the full face of the bat, and even though the bat turns in his hand, he manages to drive it to the left of mid on and pick up a boundary. Sonal Dinusha applauds from the other end. Sri Lanka's lead is now 63.
Prasidh Krishna to Keshara Nuwantha, Serves it very full, on off. Nuwantha gets his bat down and squeezes it past cover. The new ball skips across the turf before Ravindra Jadeja hunts it down with a slide as the batters pick up a couple.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, Switches to around the wicket and hits the back of a length, on off. Sonal runs it down to deep third and crosses over.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, Digs it in short, over middle. Dinusha ducks under it. The towel fell off Krishna's back, but that did not seem to put Sonal off.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, On a nagging length, on middle. Sonal gets right behind the line to defend.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, Across the off stump, on a good length. Dinusha lets the ball come on and dabs it with soft hands through point. By the time either of the two fielders in the deep can get to the ball, the batters come back for the second. The 50-run stand comes up between these two batters.
Saransh Jain to Keshara Nuwantha, A bit of turn, flatter and fuller, on middle. Keshara stays on the back foot to defend.
Saransh Jain to Keshara Nuwantha, Flat and short, on middle. Keshara Nuwantha hangs back to block it off.
Saransh Jain to Sonal Dinusha, This is tossed up by Jain, on middle. Dinusha advances down the track and tries to work it in front of square on the leg side. He goes against the turn and the ball catches a soft leading edge. It goes wide of cover for one.
Saransh Jain to Keshara Nuwantha, Drags the length back now, on off. Keshara punches it off the back foot to the man at a deep mid on and takes a quick single.
Saransh Jain to Sonal Dinusha, Attacking the front pad, on a length, Sonal paddles it behind square leg and rotates the strike.
Saransh Jain to Sonal Dinusha, Full and drifting onto the pads, a little too straight. Dinusha leans across and hangs low to play the paddle with the angle. Gets it fine of deep fine leg but it is cut off by Prasidh Krishna. A couple of runs taken, and with that, Sri Lanka's lead is now 51.
Just the one over for Siraj. Saransh Jain (19-3-59-1) has been brought back on.
Prasidh Krishna to Keshara Nuwantha, Krishna lands it full, honing in on the off stump. Nuwantha presses forward and just eases himself into the shot. Strokes it past cover but it is hauled in by Ravindra Jadeja. Two taken.
Prasidh Krishna to Keshara Nuwantha, Into the deck, angled in on middle. Keshara hops and keeps it out.
Prasidh Krishna to Keshara Nuwantha, Fuller in length, around off. Nuwantha drops his bat down on the ball and chops it down the deck.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, On a back of a length, seemed to have pitched outside the line of the leg stump. Dinusha tries to clip it away but is beaten for pace. Gets hit high on the thigh pad. A leg bye is taken as the ball goes away on the off side.
Prasidh Krishna to Keshara Nuwantha, A hint of away shape, fuller in length. Nuwantha hangs his bat out away from his body but does not push at the ball with hard hands. The ball goes quickly towards gully off the outer half. Yashasvi Jaiswal makes a half stop and it dribbles away, allowing the batters to sneak in a quick single.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, At 132.5 kph, on a back of a length, over off. Sonal stays back and drops it beside the strip on the off side with soft hands. They cross. Sri Lanka now lead by 45 runs.
Mohammed Siraj to Keshara Nuwantha, Goes wide on the crease, does Siraj. Pushes the length up, just outside the off stump. Nuwantha lets it through to the keeper.
Mohammed Siraj to Keshara Nuwantha, Angled into the right-hander, on the shorter side. Nuwantha stands tall on top of the bounce and stabs it down the deck.
Mohammed Siraj to Keshara Nuwantha, Pitches it up and gets the ball to curve away. Nuwantha resists the temptation of going for the drive and is happy to let it pass.
Mohammed Siraj to Keshara Nuwantha, Brings the line closer to the off pole, on a good length. Nuwantha makes a watchful leave.
Mohammed Siraj to Keshara Nuwantha, Drags the length back a bit but keeps it in the channel. Nuwantha shuffles across a bit to cover the off stump and shoulders arms.
Mohammed Siraj to Keshara Nuwantha, Shaping away, on a length, outside off. Nuwantha offers no shot.
It will be pace from both ends now. Here's Mohammed Siraj.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, FOUR! Beautifully played! Very full and outside the off stump, Sonal Dinusha leans completely onto the ball and handsomely drives it it square past backward point for a boundary. That's Dinusha's first four.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, A bit fuller and outside off. Dinusha gets forward and drives it to cover.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, On a nagging length, outside the off stump, Dinusha lets it be.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, Short of a good length and outside off. Dinusha shoulders arms.
India have taken the new ball. Two slips in place. There is also a man back for the pull at deep square leg.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, Full and on middle, angling in, Sonal pushes it back to the bowler.
Prasidh Krishna to Sonal Dinusha, From around the stump. Back of a length, angling in and then straightening off the pitch. Sonal Dinusha drags the bat inside the line to let it pass.
Pace is back on through Prasidh Krishna. We might see India take the new ball after Prasidh loosens up with a couple of deliveries.
Ravindra Jadeja to Sonal Dinusha, Much fuller than the previous ball, Sonal Dinusha flicks it off the pads towards deep mid-wicket for a single.
Ravindra Jadeja to Sonal Dinusha, Nice and full, around off, Dinusha watchfully blocks.

briefs.headline: Rain threat puts India’s WTC hopes under pressure in Sri Lanka Test
briefs.deck: India's prospects in the second Test against Sri Lanka loom uncertain as rain delays threaten their World Test Championship ambitions. A draw would see India slipping to fifth place, jeopardizing their path to the finals. With limited matches left, the team must secure victories to enhance their standing and continue competing at the highest level in the championships.
briefs.bodyText:
India appeared to have wrested control of the second Test against Sri Lanka after a late burst of wickets, but rain could yet play a major role in determining the outcome of the Test and, in turn, India's WTC campaign.
Sri Lanka were 218 for 6 in their second innings when play was called off early, with Sonal Dinusha and Keshara Nuwantha unbeaten at the crease. The hosts had earlier mounted a spirited fightback through Pasindu Sooriyabandara and 
Kusal Mendis
, raising the prospect of a draw if further rain disrupts the final day.
Such an outcome could hurt India's chances of making the WTC final.
India are currently fifth in the WTC standings with a points percentage of 53.33. A victory over Sri Lanka would lift 
Shubman Gill
's side to fourth place following Bangladesh's heavy defeat to Australia. A draw, however, would leave India in fifth place with their PCT slipping to 51.52.
The bigger concern is the shrinking margin for error in the remainder of the cycle.
India will have seven Tests left after this match, including a two-Test tour of New Zealand in November before a five-Test home series against Australia next year. Having already lost four of their 10 Tests in the current cycle, India can ill afford many more setbacks.
If India win seven of their remaining eight Tests, including this match, they can finish with a PCT of 68.52. But six wins and two defeats would leave them at 62.96, a figure that may not be enough based on recent qualification trends.
Three of the four teams to reach the WTC final across the last two cycles had a PCT of more than 65, with India's 58.8 in the 2023 cycle the lone exception. Both finalists in 2025 finished above 67.
The calculations also assume India do not lose any points through over-rate penalties.
For now, India remain well placed in the Test after Manav Suthar and Saransh Jain struck regularly in the final session. But with Sri Lanka still fighting and rain already interrupting play, a result remains crucial not just for the series but for India's increasingly tight road to the WTC final.

briefs.headline: Root angered by England’s off-field ‘stupid mistakes’
briefs.deck: Brydon Carse has been referred to the Cricket Regulator after videos on social media appeared to show the fast bowler being led away by police in handcuffs following an incident at a nightclub in Derby
briefs.bodyText:
Joe Root expressed his frustration that a winning return as England Test captain has been overshadowed by another off-field incident that saw Brydon Carse dropped for the second Test against Pakistan.
Carse has been referred to the Cricket Regulator after videos on social media appeared to show the fast bowler being led away by police in handcuffs following an incident at a nightclub in Derby on Saturday (August 22, 2026).
It is the latest in a series of alcohol-fuelled controversies that have dogged England since a disastrous tour of New Zealand and Australia at the end of last year.
White-ball captain Harry Brook was involved in an altercation with a nightclub bouncer in Wellington and videos circulated of opener Ben Duckett appearing drunk on a night out during the 4-1 Ashes series thrashing by Australia.
In June, former captain Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were given a written warning and stood down from the second Test against New Zealand after an incident at a London nightclub which came after they broke a curfew.
Stokes announced his shock retirement from international cricket during the third Test a few days later, paving the way for Root to return for a second spell as red-ball captain.
England thrashed Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs inside three days of his first match back in charge last week.
“If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off. I’m really disappointed that, after last week’s performance, we’re sat here and we’re talking about something that is not related to it at all,” Root told a press conference on Tuesday (August 25, 2026).
“It’s not the isolated incident itself, it’s the fact we continuously keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it’s detracting from what we are doing on the field.”
A curfew on players going out was introduced in January following the troubled tour to Down Under.
Bigger than curfews
However, Root has said he will not impose a curfew as he does not believe it is a productive way to change the culture around the England squad.
“I still don’t believe that’s the way to go. It’s important we create something bigger than that, it’s about having something long lasting that we can be proud of,” added the 35-year-old.
“Clearly we are not portraying ourselves how we want to and I think we have an opportunity to build a culture that is very strong, that we can be proud of, that is player driven and of course that isn’t going to happen overnight.
“We have already had conversations as a team on what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England, what it takes to play for England.
“We want to create something that we can be proud of, that people who follow us can be proud of.”
Carse was not selected for the first Test and has been withdrawn from the squad for the second Test, which begins at Lord’s on Thursday (August 27, 2026).
Former England captain Michael Vaughan believes an example has to be made to draw a line in the sand and improve off-field behaviour going forward.
“Someone is going to have to get a punishment that sends a shiver down the whole England cricket team and right down through the programme, so that everyone knows that if you misbehave or bring any kind of bad reputation onto this team, you know what’s going to come,” Vaughan told the BBC.
“It’s the only punishment that will really hurt players.”

briefs.headline: Eng vs Pak Test: England eyes series sweep, Babar returns for Pakistan
briefs.deck: England ought to be in an utterly buoyant mood after returning captain Joe Root oversaw an innings and 103-run thrashing of Pakistan inside three days at his Headingley homeground last week
briefs.bodyText:
England will aim to put their latest drinking drama behind them when they face Pakistan in the second Test at Lord’s starting on Thursday (August 27, 2026).
The hosts ought to be in an utterly buoyant mood after returning captain Joe Root oversaw an innings and 103-run thrashing of Pakistan inside three days at his Headingley homeground last week.
But rather than speak about England’s progress, Root spent much of a pre-match press conference talking about Brydon Carse, dropped from the squad and now under investigation by the Cricket Regulator after videos on social media showed the fast bowler being led away by police in handcuffs following an incident at a Derby nightclub on Saturday (August 22, 2026).
This is the latest in a series of alcohol-fuelled controversies that have dogged England since a disastrous 2025/26 tour of New Zealand and Australia.
Both former captain Ben Stokes — who has since retired from all international cricket — and paceman Gus Atkinson were stood down in June from the second Test at home to New Zealand following an incident at a London bar which came after they broke a curfew policy that has now been ditched by Root.
Carse did not feature at Headingley, and was unlikely to play at Lord’s barring injury, but his conduct led a frustrated Root to say Tuesday: “If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off...It’s not the isolated incident itself, it’s the fact we continuously keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it’s detracting from what we are doing on the field.”
England, with seamers Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue taking eight wickets apiece, skittled out Pakistan for just 171 and 135 in the first Test while posting 409 themselves, even though none of their four batsmen who reached fifty, a quartet including Root, went on to a century.
Nevertheless, it was a professional display lacking the self-indulgent extravagances that characterised England’s cricket in the closing stages of the Bazball era under Stokes and Brendon McCullum, sacked as Test coach following the series loss to New Zealand.
Pakistan ‘hopeful’ over Babar Azam
By contrast, Pakistan were deficient in all departments with their inadequate batting compounded by an inaccurate and largely unthreatening pace attack as well as embarrassingly shoddy fielding.
Pakistan captain Babar Azam, however, could return at Lord’s from a finger injury initially sustained during the tour of the West Indies and later exacerbated when he was hit on the hand during a warm-up game at Beckenham.
“We’re hopeful he will be available for the game and today (Tuesday) he was looking good; he batted well in the nets,” said Pakistan bowling coach Umar Gul. “He had a full batting session.”
Azam was Pakistan’s top run-scorer in the West Indies, with 193 runs during a drawn two-Test series.
He has also enjoyed success in England, with three fifties in six innings while averaging 65.75.
Azan Awais may make way if Azam returns at number four, with one of Shan Masood or Abdullah Shafique moving up the order to open.
Pakistan, who only a decade ago were Test cricket’s top-ranked side, have won their last two Tests at Lord’s, with Azam making 68 during a nine-wicket rout of England in 2018.
But even though Pakistan have a longstanding reputation for veering between astonishing highs and lows, a vast improvement will be required if they are to level this three-match series.
“We’ll have to learn from the mistakes we made in the previous game,” said Gul. “If you want to win a Test match, you have to perform in all departments. One can’t be carrying the other.”
Meanwhile, with England having won just three of their last 11 Tests, a wary Root said: “We know the individual brilliance that lies within that team and what Pakistan are capable of collectively.
“We also know that whenever we play anyone at Lord’s, they generally raise their game. This (England) group won’t be taking anything for granted.”
Published - August 27, 2026 03:44 am IST
